column1: # THE OPEN QUESTIONS, AS ROWS. Extracted 7 October 2026 from the prose of /open-questions/.
# *** WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. *** The page was 188 lines of prose: seven questions and two blocked
# routes, none of it reachable by a filter, countable by a gate, or comparable with the other archives
# in this estate. The kit's Questions component takes rows of {q, state, known, tried, settles} and its
# own docstring says why the extraction could not be done from outside - it is "research work belonging
# to each archive rather than something to guess at from outside".
# *** NOTHING WAS DROPPED IN THE MOVE, and that was the whole risk. *** The long panel under question 1
# - the Lerena-Lerena compound test, the forty-three transcription doublings, the Carmen Lerena act
# read off film 007713392 image 2511, and the sentence that says the test LOWERS the probability
# without settling it - is carried into `tried` in full. A question that loses its negative evidence
# in a refactor is worse than a question left as prose.
# THE FIELDS HOLD HTML, which is what the component expects. Internal links carry the /TheLerena base
# because these cells are not passed through u().
# `state`: open | blocked. Two rows are BLOCKED rather than open - they are not questions about the
# family at all, but routes that failed, and the page kept them under "Recorded so they are not
# repeated". They keep that meaning here.
# *** ONE ASYMMETRY THAT COST A BUILD: *** the `href` COLUMN is passed through the kit's u(),
# which adds the /TheLerena base, but the HTML inside `known`, `tried` and `settles` is NOT - it is

column2: Who were Juan Carlos and María Lerena?
column4: The question this archive exists to answer. Everything else on this page is secondary to it.
column5: Pablo Armando’s army enrolment card of 1908 names his parents: Juan Carlos Lerena and María Lerena. Nothing else is known of either of them — not a date, not a marriage, not a death. María is written with her husband’s surname: on these cards hijo de X y de Y usually gives each parent’s own name, which would make her a Lerena by birth and the marriage one between kin — but some clerks used the married name, and the card cannot tell. And the one Lerena in the whole Rosario register, folio 229 of February 1866, says of both parents “naturales del E. Oriental” — Uruguayan.
column6: Both volumes of the Rosario baptism index, read end to end, 1731 to 1901. The surname appears once in a hundred and seventy years. 1881, 1882 and 1883 were also swept across all twenty-six letter sections for a Pablo Armando under any surname. He is not there; neither is his family, before him or after him. The Rosario confirmation register, read page by page from 15 May 1885 to the 1897 section — about two and a half thousand children, every entry naming both parents — and no Lerena under any of seven spellings. He was three when it opens and fifteen when it closes. The Arquidiócesis de Montevideo dispensation register, 1856–1932, searched by its own formulae: eight Lerena dispensations in seventy-six years, and no Juan Carlos and no Lerena–Lerena pairing at all. Every Lerena in it marries out — Fernández, Peláez, Álvarez, Cordero, Márquez. That is a weak negative, filed as one: the register records only exceptions, and an ordinary marriage between unrelated people leaves no trace in it. And the sharpest test there is, run 14 September 2026. A child of two Lerenas carries both surnames, so the compound Lerena Lerena was run — four documents against the Uruguayan registers, forty-three against the whole transcribed corpus. Every one was opened. All forty-three are transcription doublings — the machine repeating a word across a line or page break — and the only genuine compounds are Colombian, a different family on a different continent. One of them was then checked against the act rather than the transcript: film 007713392 image 2511, Cementerio del Cordón. The margin reads simply “Carmen Lerena” and the body “hija legítima de Justo Lerena y de Juana Quinta[na]” — one Lerena parent. The compound exists only in the machine. The index is also a year out, giving 1840 where the act reads mil ochocientos cuarenta y uno. What that does not do is close the question. A woman can be a Lerena by birth without her children ever being written so, and full text reaches only what has been transcribed, which at Rosario de Santa Fe is thin. It lowers the probability; it does not settle it — and it means no Lerena–Lerena marriage should be asserted anywhere in this archive. And the drawer itself, read end to end on 10 September 2026 — which this page went on describing as unread for a month. Cajón 985’s Lerena section runs from the hand-lettered guide card “Lere. n.” at image 663 to the end of the run at 688, and every card in it was read for its indexed parents. Twenty cards, and not one names a Juan Carlos Lerena except Pablo Armando’s own. The drawer is also not filed alphabetically, as this page used to say — it is grouped by SOUND, with Lera, Lerena, Lorena, Serena, Sera, Era, Leza, Perena, Perella and Hereijo interfiled, which is why the index’s manglings survived in it. The fathers were then traced on 13 September: three branches, every one Uruguayan or married in Uruguay — Gilberto Lerena Lenguas (Montevideo, 1855), Alejandro M. Lerena (Uruguay, 1844) and Nemesio Ramón (married at Salto, 1903) — settling in Entre Ríos, Misiones and Buenos Aires. None is Juan Carlos and none is shown to be his kin. What that buys is a base rate, not a link: in this generation an Argentine Lerena is a Uruguayan family’s son far more often than not, and a Juan Carlos who left no trace at Rosario fits that shape. And the register was tested against its own index. Rosario cathedral’s baptisms were read act by act from the margins at full resolution, 1 February to 2 August 1882 — 798 consecutive baptisms, no Lerena in any spelling — so wherever the 1945 typescript says there is none, the book agrees. Both Rosario confirmation registers, the Catedral and Santa Rosa de Lima, are now complete, and he is in neither. And on 9 October one of those fathers was traced. A parent-pair query on the wife’s distinctive surname — LERENA with spouse CARNIGLIA — cut the crowd to three records in one search, and the first of them, a baptism at the Iglesia Matriz de Mendoza on 6 January 1900, calls Carlos Lerena and Adela Carniglia orientales — and a second act, two years later and on a printed form, names the city: both natural de Montevideo. That makes four traceable fathers in that drawer and every one of them Uruguayan or married in Uruguay. It names nobody, but it sharpens the base rate against which a Juan Carlos who left no trace at Rosario should be read. And on 10 October the pattern broke. Arturo Lerena García, the last of the drawer’s fathers to be worked, is Spanish — a journalist, married to a Peruvian, with children born in La Pampa, Valparaíso, Mendoza, Buenos Aires and Entre Ríos. A drawer holding a Spaniard and a Peruvian is a drawer of immigrants, not a drawer of Uruguayans, and the inference about Juan Carlos weakens accordingly. He is also the first documented Spanish-born Lerena this archive has found in Argentina, and his mother’s surname is known — García — which is the shape question 5 has been asking for.
column7: A Uruguayan Lerena line holding a Juan Carlos born in the 1840s or 1850s, married to a María. That is still the single most useful thing a stranger could tell this archive. The three untraced fathers of Cajón 985: the drawer has been read, and of the men named on its cards as fathers three still have no established origin. A fourth, Carlos Lerena, was traced on 9 October — a second daughter’s Mendoza baptism of 23 April 1902, on a printed form with a natural de blank, makes him natural de Montevideo, and his wife too. Two Lerenas stood godparent to his children and neither came — an Avelino Lerena in 1900 and a Mercedes Lerena de Martínez in 1902, both by proxy. Two of the three were searched on 10 October and the result is withdrawn: those searches ran on a FamilySearch session that had silently signed out, which returns a restricted tier for every query. They are neither traced nor excluded, and both must be redone signed in. Corrections → Leandro Lorena (wife Llanos) was searched and nothing can yet be concluded — the control that protected that search passed before it and failed after it. Concepción Lerena, who appears as a mother with no father named, is in the same position — but her son’s 1899 Mendoza baptism should lie in a book this archive has already read twice — Santiago Apóstol y San Nicolás, Baptism Records 1899–1901 — and that is a page-by-page read, not a search. And Arturo Lerena García is traced: his son’s Entre Ríos marriage of 1924 makes him Spanish and a journalist, living at Paraná, in his fifties, married to a Peruvian. That breaks the pattern this page was leaning on. Five of the drawer’s fathers can now be traced and they are not all Uruguayan — only not Argentine. So the base rate behind “a Juan Carlos who left no trace at Rosario fits the Uruguayan shape” is weaker than it looked, and this question says so rather than quietly keeping the stronger version. Corrections → The consular matrícula: a man enrolling at the Cape Town consulate in 1908 had a file there, and the request to the Archivo Histórico de Cancillería was lodged on 9 September 2026 and has not yet been answered.

column2: Was he really a Consul General?
column5: The family and several later records call Pablo Armando a Consul General. The archive has not tested the claim against any official list.
column7: The Government Gazette for the exequatur — the host state’s formal recognition of a foreign consul, which is crisp, dated and decisive. The Argentine Boletín Oficial and the Foreign Ministry’s diplomatic lists for the appointment. And which post: Cape Town, Johannesburg, Pretoria or Durban, and in which years. One hypothesis worth testing first: an honorary consul — a resident merchant holding the post — would appear in the gazettes but not in the career foreign-service lists, and would reconcile a diplomat with a man who bred horses and farmed ostriches.

column5: Pablo Armando trained and owned racehorses at the Cape, and the family tradition is that he imported from Argentina.
column7: The South African Stud Book and Jockey Club registers for Lerena as owner, breeder or importer — particularly imports from Argentina, which would corroborate the claim directly. The Argentine Stud Book at the other end. Who Gilberto Justiniano Lerena Lenguas was in family terms — his dates, household and descendants — and whether he connects to this line at all. And Haras El Viejo: its records, its sale or dispersal, and its succession.

column5: The family holds that there was an ostrich farm. Nothing documentary has been found for it.
column7: The Oudtshoorn and Little Karoo farm records, and the C.P. Nel Museum’s holdings on the feather trade. The deeds registry, for land held under the surname. And a date test that constrains more than the farm: the feather boom collapsed in 1914, so if the farm was real it most likely predates that — which in turn constrains when the family arrived.

column5: Two theories of the surname’s origin. Forebears summarises the Spanish Lerenas as chiefly La Rioja, Andalusia and Madrid — which is awkward for both, and is a summary rather than the real figures.
column6: Forebears’ Spain page for the surname returned no content to an automated fetch, so the provincial breakdown still rests on the summary.
column7: The INE provincial distribution for Spain, or a read by hand. Lerena and Llerena alternating for the same individual in River Plate records — that, more than any etymology, settles whether the two names are one. And the emigration record, which normally names the town of origin outright.

column5: Pablo Armando was born at Rosario de Santa Fe on 22 February 1882 and died at Newlands, Cape Town, in 1950. Neither the family’s arrival in Argentina nor its departure for South Africa is dated.
column6: The Rosario baptism and confirmation registers have both been swept end to end and hold neither him nor his family — see question 1.
column7: Santa Fe civil registration and the Rosario parish registers. CEMLA and the Buenos Aires passenger lists, for the arrival from Europe. The outbound crossing to South Africa — the date, the ship, and who travelled. And keep Uruguay live throughout: it has the world’s densest Lerena population, and if Argentina stalls it is the next move, not the last resort.

column5: There are 61 South African Lerenas. Whether they are one family, and whether this line founded it, is untested.
column7: Whether the 61 are indeed one family and whether this line founded it. The Booyzen marriage — an Afrikaner connection, and evidence of settlement rather than a posting. And whether Taylor and Barry attach to this line or to another branch of the tree.
